videos.title: The Jazz Trumpeter Behind Neo-Soul's Greatest Era
videos.description:
Even if you don't recognize his name, you've heard his sound. Jazz trumpeter Roy Hargrove played trumpet on, and contributed arrangements to, D'Angelo's Voodoo, Common's Like Water for Chocolate, and Erykah Badu's Mama's Gun. He was equally at home with neo-soul and hip-hop, and straight-ahead acoustic jazz. At the same time he was contributing to era-defining Soulquarian projects, he was producing music with his jazz quintet.

Today, jazz pianists Adam Maness and Peter Martin listen to his 2008 masterpiece Earfood and explore why it may be the perfect jazz album for the jazz-curious neo-soul fan.

videos.title: Jazz pianists still hear something new in Black Messiah, 12 years later
videos.description:
D'Angelo's Black Messiah is one of the greatest albums of the 21st century. You can hear his musical influences all over it: Prince's arrangements, the Bee Gees' falsettos, Jimi Hendrix's guitar, Sly's groove. But the alchemy that makes Black Messiah so powerful could only come from one mind: D'Angelo, the artist who gave us Voodoo and Brown Sugar.

Jazz pianists Adam Maness and Peter Martin unpack D'Angelo and the Vanguard's Black Messiah track by track, detailing what their trained ears hear in the music, and highlighting new textures, harmonies, and song structures you may have missed on the first listen. 

Plus, Peter shares stories about his friendship and working relationship with legendary trumpet player Roy Hargrove.

Featuring Bill Evans on piano, Scott LaFaro on bass and Paul Motian on drums, this 1962 live album has become the template for every AI jazz playlist. And yet, it stands apart as one of the greatest jazz piano trio albums of all time. Pianists Adam Maness and Peter Martin listen to the full album, track-by-track, describing what they hear in the music that lends this album its undeniable humanity.

videos.description:

So we're upping the stakes ... with a draft. Adam and Peter each present their top tracks from Songs in the Key of Life, compare and contrast, and see who comes out on top with the best lineup.

videos.title: Kind of Blue Isn't Perfect. It's Better
videos.description:
Miles Davis's Kind of Blue is one of the greatest albums of all time - possibly THE greatest. But it's not perfect. 

In this special episode of You'll Hear It, jazz pianists Peter Martin and Adam Maness break down this classic record, track-by-track, to uncover why it has become so legendary. They dig into what's really going on in the music during this album's best moments: Miles's trumpet solo on "So What", Wynton Kelly's piano solo on "Freddie Freeloader", John Coltrane's entrance on "Blue in Green".

Plus - we learn more about what Miles was doing in his early years, his break from bebop, what he thought of Bill Evans's approach, and the production and engineering techniques that give Kind of Blue its unique sound.

Miles Davis was born just outside of St. Louis 100 years ago this week. To celebrate his centennial birthday, Adam and Peter filmed this episode in front of a live audience at The Sheldon Concert Hall in St. Louis, MO.

videos.title: The Two Days That MADE Miles
videos.description:
Cookin', Relaxin', Workin', and Steamin' capture Miles Davis on one of music history's most remarkable upswings. He had recently become clean after a years-long heroin addiction that led to his exclusion from major record labels and clubs. And now, in 1956, he had a deal with Columbia - the Cadillac of record labels - and a band he loved: Red Garland on piano, Philly Joe Jones on drums, Paul Chambers on bass and John Coltrane playing the sax. 

In this episode of You'll Hear It, jazz pianists Peter Martin and Adam Maness go through each album. They discuss the outsized influence of Ahmad Jamal, Red Garland's Red spread technique, the power of Miles's chatter on Relaxin' and whether this is the greatest rhythm section in the history of recorded music. 

Whether this is your first introduction to Miles Davis, or you've been listening to these albums for years, you'll walk away from this episode with a new understanding of, and appreciation for, Miles and his first great quintet.

videos.title: The Album Marvin DIDN'T Write Might Be His Best Work
videos.description:
Marvin Gaye's I Want You could be one of his greatest albums, and he didn't even write it. Producer Leon Ware wrote most of the songs for himself. Marvin Gaye was only supposed to record the title track. But he heard Leon playing a demo of the album one night and stayed up listening until morning. The next day, he asked Ware if he could have the whole thing.

In this episode, Peter and Adam break down why the title track, "I Want You", might be one of his best songs, and whether the rest of the album can possibly live up to it.

This episode was recorded before the passing of James Gadson (June 17, 1939 – April 2, 2026), the drummer on I Want You. Gadson was one of the defining session drummers of 1970s soul. He was the drummer behind "Lean On Me," "I Will Survive," "Express Yourself", and the groove that powers this very album. Rest in peace, James.

videos.title: The Accidental Album that Became a Global Phenomenon
videos.description:
Buena Vista Social Club: The album so good it's life-affirming. And it almost didn't happen.

In 1996, an American musician landed in Cuba to record a music project with Malian musicians. But when they didn't show up, Ry Cooder and his producer, Juan de Marcos González, went looking for replacements. 

That's when they found Compay Segundo, Ibrahim Ferrer and Rubén González, who had seen their musical prime decades earlier in the 40s and 50s. Compay was nearing his 90s, and some believed he had died, until he showed up on Buena Vista Social Club. Rubén hadn't played in years, and didn't even own a piano. 

But together with a cast of all-star Cuban musicians, they created what would become the best-selling world music album of all time. 

How did Buena Vista Social Club become a global phenomenon? 

In this episode of You'll Hear It, Peter Martin and Adam Maness listen to the record track-by-track to understand what makes this album so magnetic, and how it holds up 30 years later. Plus - a FIRST in You'll Hear It history.

videos.title: Is This the Most Controversial Jazz Album in History?
videos.description:
Ornette Coleman's The Shape of Jazz to Come (1959) may be the most controversial album in jazz history, and one of the most important.

In 1959, a broke musician from Fort Worth, Texas arrived in New York City with a plastic saxophone and a band that didn't play by the rules. And EVERYONE had an opinion about it.

Jazz legends hated it. Miles Davis said Ornette was "all screwed up inside." Max Roach punched him in the mouth. Dizzy Gillespie said Ornette's music wasn't even jazz. Meanwhile, Leonard Berstein and John Coltrane celebrated him.

So what exactly is The Shape of Jazz to Come, and why was it so radical? Jazz pianists Peter Martin and Adam Maness break down every track, from "Lonely Woman" to "Chronology". They dig into harmolodics, free jazz, and how Ornette shaped everyone from Miles Davis (who eventually came around) to the '80s burnout crew, including Wynton Marsalis, who personally recommended this record to Peter.

Dig into The Shape of Jazz to Come with us, and learn why this soft spoken saxophonist inspired both criticism and awe.

videos.title: The Charlie Parker Album We Don't Talk About Enough
videos.description:
Charlie Parker was punk rock before there was punk rock. His bebop was underground music: subversive, intellectual, and a major departure from popular music of the day (think: Nat King Cole, The Andrews Sisters, Perry Como). He was an intellectual heavyweight, nearly untouchable in his technical ability and pushing music to places no one else was daring to go. So where did Charlie Parker with Strings, his most accessible album, come from?

It's not Bird going commercial, like some have claimed. Charlie Parker with Strings is an album he fought to make. He loved Bach and Stravinsky (even quoting the opening of Stravinsky's 'Firebird Suite' mid-solo in one legendary performance), and had longed to make a record where his jazz saxophone was accompanied by strings.

The resulting record is music's greatest improviser at his best. Jazz pianists Peter Martin and Adam Maness listen to select tracks (like "Just Friends" and "Summertime"), breaking down the theory behind the music to understand what makes this album great.

On today's episode of You'll Hear It, jazz pianists Peter Martin and Adam Maness are breaking down the 1980 album track by track: the jazz harmony hiding inside those smooth grooves, the abstract poetry of the lyrics, and the insane stories behind how this thing got made. And after all that, we didn't get another Steely Dan record for 20 years.

Was it worth it?

videos.title: Why You Should Love Tapestry (Even If You Don’t Know Why)
videos.description:
Carole King’s Tapestry is so cozy, you'll want to hug it, sit with it. It sounds simple, warm, and totally unassuming. But it’s way more impressive than it seems at first.

Adam and Peter break down what’s actually going on beneath the surface of Tapestry ... and what most people miss. 

Carole King was already an elite songwriter long before this album. You know Aretha Franklin's “(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman”? Carole wrote that. “Will You Love Me Tomorrow” by The Shirelles? She wrote that, too. When she was just 17! 

Listen closely and you hear it everywhere: in her chords; in the way the she actually PLAYS the piano instead of just accompanying her vocals; and in the way her melodies and lyrics lock together so naturally you barely notice how intentional it all is. 

Add in that soulful, sweet voice, and you start to understand how this unassuming record became a chart-topping, Grammy-dominating classic when it came out in 1971.

Tapestry sounds easy, but it's not. Check out this episode, and you'll never hear this album the same way again.

videos.description:
Keith Jarrett's "The Köln Concert" is the best selling solo piano album of all time. But why this album? Possibly because it sounded like nothing else in popular music at the time of its release in 1975. "The Köln Concert" is cinematic, genre-fluid and masterful – in many ways ahead of its time.

Jazz musicians Adam Maness and Peter Martin listen to one of the most popular albums in the history of jazz, pulling apart all the elements that make it great: the melodies, the vamps, even the "soul" of Jarrett's notoriously flawed piano.

If you know "The Köln Concert" well, watch for the analysis and hot takes. If you haven't heard this album before, it may just become the soundtrack to your life!

videos.title: Roy Hargrove’s “Hard Groove” Started a Jazz Revolution
videos.description:
The RH Factor’s Hard Groove might sound uncontroversial to modern ears, but in the early 2000s it was revolutionary. With this record, Roy Hargrove broke away from the straight-ahead jazz revival of the Young Lions era and created something entirely new. Hard Groove blended Roy’s trumpet with the voices of R&B and soul heavyweights like D’Angelo, Erykah Badu, and Common, artists whose platinum-selling albums (Voodoo, Mama’s Gun, Like Water for Chocolate) already featured Roy’s melodic horn playing and orchestral arrangements.

With Hard Groove, Roy flipped the script: instead of lending his sound to the hip hop and neo-soul world, he invited those artists onto a jazz record. The result was a landmark project that blurred genres and redefined what jazz could be in the 21st century.

videos.title: Why Rumours Still Captivates After All These Years?
videos.description:
Fleetwood Mac's Rumours is undoubtedly one of the best pop rock albums ever. But the story behind its creation reads like a soap opera. Everyone -- Stevie Nicks, Lindsey Buckingham, Christine McVie, John McVie, and Mic Fleetwood -- were enduring heartbreak during its recording. Stevie and Lindsey were breaking up. The McVies had already split, but John wasn't ready to let go. Even Mic Fleetwood was separating from his wife back home. For three months, they were stuck in a recording booth together nearly round the clock, singing each other's breakup songs and harmonizing with their exes. 

Heartbreak is encoded in every song, from Lindsey Buckingham's "Never Going Back Again" to Christine McVie's "You Make Loving Fun" to Stevie Nick's "Dreams". But in spite of ... or maybe because of? ... this turmoil, Rumours has become one the best selling albums of all time. 

Peter and Adam listen to this pop rock masterpiece front-to-back, deconstructing each song (and the stories behind them) to understand what makes this album great.

videos.title: Why Maiden Voyage is (Almost) Herbie's Greatest Album
videos.description:
Today we're going on an aquatic journey with Herbie Hancock's Maiden Voyage. Herbie calls the title track the best tune he's ever written.  We dive deep into the music to explore what makes this tune, and this album, great. 

The roots of Maiden Voyage date back in 1963, when Herbie began hearing rumors that Miles Davis wanted to hear him play. He didn't believe it at first -- Miles was at the height of his celebrity by this point. But soon he got a call. He went over to Miles's house and played with him, George Coleman, Tony Williams and Ron Carter for three days. On the third day, Miles asks the group to come to studio to record Seven Steps to Heaven. Herbie says, "Does that mean I'm in the band?" Miles says, "You're making the record, mother f**cker!" 

After two years playing in what many call the one of the greatest jazz ensembles of all time, Herbie would release Maiden Voyage in 1965. Along with George, Tony and Ron, plus trumpeter Freddie Hubbard. Although it is one of his simplest tunes -- with a rhythm inspired by a cologne commercial -- Maiden Voyage would become a favorite and a standard among jazz musicians.

videos.title: Is Keith Jarrett The Greatest Solo Pianist Ever?
videos.description:
One afternoon in Oslo changed the course of jazz piano history! In this episode, Adam and Peter dive into Facing You, the hit 1971 ECM release where a 26-year-old Keith Jarrett – torn between Miles Davis’ electric band and his own acoustic instincts – walked alone into a studio and recorded eight completely improvised masterpieces. From the gospel-tinged “In Front” to the apex moment in “Lalene,” we explore his remarkable touch, bluesy intuition, and the distinctive distorted Steinway that producer Manfred Eicher perfectly captured. We place this album among solo piano giants (Monk, Tatum, Evans), lovingly examine Jarrett’s “fussy” reputation, and show how this afternoon session laid the blueprint for his legendary Köln Concert. Five decades later, we jazz pianists are still chasing the magic Keith created that day.

videos.title: The Ten Most Important Years In Jazz
videos.description:
Take a trip with us to the most revolutionary decade in jazz (1923-1933... ok, 11 years 😅), when a young Louis Armstrong was creating a new improvisational vocabulary in real-time. This isn’t the “Wonderful World” Satchmo most know, but the young gunner whose genius trumpet solos on “West End Blues” and “Tight Like This” were toppling trumpet kings. We break down Pops’ evolution from King Oliver’s second to pioneering frontman, explore his inventive scat singing (supposedly born when he dropped his lyric sheet), and trace how his massive popularity caught the attention of Chicago gangsters – careful now! From his recordings with Earl “Fatha” Hines to “Black and Blue” – the first jazz song addressing racism – hear exactly why we say there would be no jazz without Louis Armstrong.

videos.title: Miles' Greatest Album - You're Welcome
videos.description:
Could Miles Davis’ peak performance come alongside a bunch of kids who weren’t even getting paid? In this episode, Peter and Adam dive into one of the greatest live albums ever captured, My Funny Valentine: Live at the Philharmonic (1964). We explore how Miles Davis, sideman George Coleman, and a young rhythm section (Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter, and teenage Tony Williams) made jazz history in real time with their one-of-a-kind (unpaid) voter registration benefit concert. Learn how the quintet remade Miles’ go-to standards (“All of You”, “Stella”, “All Blues”...) with their conversational, free-flowing, spacious playing – and hear the evolution across Davis’ career. Join us as we break down these incredible performances and prove why this underappreciated live album captures Miles’ greatest playing ever (at least for Peter’s ears).

In this episode, we’re looking at early 60's Bill alongside Scott LaFaro and Paul Motian, and the four albums they recorded together before LaFaro’s tragic death at just 25 years old. videos.title: How Fela Kuti Turned Music Into a Weapon - DUAL SCREEN AUTO SYNC
videos.description:
This is a Dual Screen Experience! You'll need to watch this on a TV or Computer and also have your phone - otherwise this video won't make much sense. 

Use your phone to head to https://sync.diggingthegreats.com/watch/fela-kuti-companion-video to automatically sync the accompanying video. Full explanation in the video above - let me know how you enjoyed this format! 

Note: there are strategically placed YouTube ads in between each section of this video and you'll need to hit stop on your phone during an ad break, and then just hit play to resync again once the video continues. If you have YouTube Premium, you DO NOT need to stop your phone at any point. 

This is a re-release of the Fela Kuti video that automatically syncs the companion video. To watch the manual sync video, click here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TqTn-aS9W04

If you don’t know who Fela Kuti is, I’m about to introduce you to your new favorite artist. If you’re familiar with him already, you know he invented a new genre of music called Afrobeat, combining funk, jazz, and West African rhythms, but that’s only half of the story. The other half is what his music stood for. Today we’re diving into the music and world of Fela Kuti, and we’ll see how he created some of the best music ever made, gave hope to people for generations, and nearly toppled a dictatorship.

Thanks to Jad Abumrad for chatting with me. Go check out his podcast "Fela Kuti: Fear No Man" wherever you listen to podcasts! https://podcasts.ap

videos.title: The Weird Way Cassette Tapes BROKE REALITY (Mixtape Ep. 2)
videos.description:
Vote for Mixtape to Win a Webby Award: https://wbby.co/57585N

Welcome back to Mixtape, my 4 part series about how cassette tapes changed the world. I’ve been listening to music exclusively on cassettes, and collecting stories about tapes, trying to figure out why they’re seeing a comeback. What I’ve found is mind blowing. 

New technologies are just first drafts - what we actually DO with them is the real story. 

Today I have two stories that push this idea in opposite directions. One shows how an art form built on cassettes settled into something simpler. The other shows how the same magnetic particles that captured “reality” ended up breaking it. 

Cassette sales are at a 20 year high, but don’t call it a comeback - we live in a world reshaped by how we chose to use magnetic tape.

__________________________________

videos.title: The Funk Opera That Changed Music: Parliament's Mothership Connection
videos.description:
Sign up for Camp Digs for FREE at http://www.patreon.com/diggingthegreats

In 1975 Parliament released the album “Mothership Connection” an album that would cement the group in the history books, inspiring generations of musicians for decades. It’s somehow  simultaneously timeless, but also VERY of it’s time. Today we’re diving into this album: the story, the sounds, the influence, and also the time it came out of, and seeing how Parliament went on to be one of the most important bands in music history. So put a glide in your stride, and a dip in your hip, and come on up to the mothership!

videos.description:
Thank you to Bombas for sponsoring this video! Head to https://bombas.com/diggingthegreats and use code DIGGINGTHEGREATS at checkout for 20% off your first purchase.

Lupe Fiasco’s 2006 song “Kick, Push” is a classic, and the first official single of his career, putting him on the map - but - the song was never actually meant to be a single. videos.title: Why "Random Access Memories" is a MASTERPIECE
videos.description:
Daft Punk’s “Random Access Memories” was released in 2013, and it 2021 they announced they they had disbanded - but listening through this album - it’s clear that, this was ALWAYS going to be their last album. While their 2001 album “Discovery” has a ton of samples, and comes to a head on the song “Face to Face” where they’re essentially playing like 8 different sampled as it’s own instrument - Random Access Memories mirrors that with Daft Punk sampling… humans. 

I know that “Sampling Humans” sounds like a horror movie, but stick with me, we’re gonna unpack this ENTIRE album, all 14 tracks - YES 14! There’s a bonus track that you may not have heard - and see how this album is a masterpiece about love, music, humanity, robots, looking back on their career, and blasting off into new… Horizons.

videos.title: Native Tongues
De La Soul, Tribe & Jungle Bros Changed Hip Hop
videos.description:
The Native Tongues represent an expansion within hip hop - a new musical sub-genre with a new focus. It’s an incredibly influential period of music history. It's also some of best music ever made.  

Stream the Spotify Listening Guide: https://open.spotify.com/playlist/7mPwS3bSXTDF2BsoWDmpUL?si=cadeec9708e64020

ADDITIONAL NOTES
At 1:05 - "Nixon's War on Drugs" - this is larger than just one President, as the "War on Drugs" was started in 1971 with Nixon (Controlled Substances Act, creating the DEA) but was expanded by Reagan  (zero tolerance policies and increases penalties, resulting in an increase of non-violent drug offenders (predominantly Black Men) behind bars). This is a very large issue that spans decades and we're still seeing the results of today. While Reagan expanded the War on Drugs and was President in 1988 when Straight Outta Compton was released, the War on Drugs is larger than just him, so I chose the wording of "Nixon's War on Drugs" 

At 10:19 - I misspoke - instead of Pharrell, I mean Kanye, who produced John Legend's "Get Lifted"

videos.title: The Musical Movement We Don't Talk About Enough
videos.description:

videos.title: When James Brown INCEPTED Hip Hop

videos.title: Playing with Chick Corea | Stanley Clarke on The Questlove Show
videos.description:
Philly's own Stanley Clarke, one of the bassists who plugged in and moved the instrument to the front of the stage, finally joins Questlove to retrace his career. He looks back on growing up in Philadelphia, his strict classical training at Settlement Music School and the day Chick Corea talked him out of joining the orchestra to start Return to Forever. Stanley also tells the story behind his 1-of-1 Alembic bass, explains why Larry Graham is the most important electric bassist ever and remembers his close friendship with Jaco Pastorius.                                                                                                                        

Then come the wild stories: touring with Keith Richards and Ronnie Wood in the New Barbarians, recording with Aretha Franklin and getting a songwriting credit from Paul McCartney. He also explains how a Pee-wee's Playhouse gig grew into a film-scoring career, including the Boyz n the Hood screaming saxophone cue that's suddenly viral 35 years later. It's a deep look at courage, freedom and making music that changes minds. 

Stanley Clarke's new box set, Last Train to Sanity [https://lasttraintosanity.com/], is available now.

videos.title: Iconic Songs About the End | Lenny Kaye on The Questlove Show
videos.description:
Before the Ramones and the Sex Pistols, Lenny Kaye was clerking at Village Oldies on Bleecker Street. In 1972, he compiled Nuggets—and its liner notes helped shape the emerging idea of Punk Rock.

Questlove and Lenny nerd out as fellow record obsessives, swapping stories about organizing vinyl, seeing Jimi Hendrix twice, meeting Patti Smith (whom he played bass for ever since), and recording “Piss Factory” in the final 15 minutes of a session at Electric Lady. Lenny also talks about his new solo debut, Goin' Local [https://lennykaye.lnk.to/GoinLocal], out now on Yep Roc. Made for artistic closure, not to chase a trend, the personal, unhurried record came from a simple conviction: “because I’m my favorite artist.” He reflects on creativity, his enduring love of music, and the crates he’s digging through now.

videos.title: Luther Vandross Covering Superstar | Nat Adderley Jr on The Questlove Show
videos.description:
For Nat Adderley Jr., serving as Luther Vandross’ musical director and longtime pianist was one chapter in a remarkable musical life—and a partnership that helped shape the sound of modern R&B. In conversation with Questlove, Nat looks back on making “Never Too Much,” flying in from Houston to play “A House Is Not a Home,” and trying to talk Luther out of recording the Carpenters’ version of “Superstar.” As Vandross is inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, Nat recalls the grandeur of Luther’s stage shows and the loss of drummer Yogi
Horton. He also reflects on how his arrangement of “If This World Were Mine” found new life in Kendrick Lamar’s “Luther.”

The funny, unpredictable conversation also touches on Nat’s new album, Took So Long [https://linktr.ee/natadderleyjr]—his first as a leader and a return to the Jazz roots that run through his family and his work. In a personal full-circle moment, Quest' tells Nat how a
protest song Nat recorded at 15 with his uncle Cannonball Adderley changed his life.

#TheQuestloveShow #Questlove #TheQuestloveShowPodcast #QuestloveShow #QuestloveSupreme #iHeartPodcasts #Podcast #luthervandross #NatAdderleyJr #jazz

videos.title: Infinity Song in Central Park
videos.description:
The Questlove Show welcomes Infinity Song's Abraham, Angel, and Israel Boyd. The Detroit-born siblings spent years busking at Central Park's Bethesda Fountain before signing with Roc Nation and earning the support of some of music and film's biggest stars.

The three Boyds talk about being homeschooled by a mom who handed out sour gummy candy watches as rewards for grammar drills, learning harmony as section leaders in their dad's choir, and moving to New York in 2006 out of necessity rather than in pursuit of a dream. Infinity Song also discusses rebuilding the band after founding member Victory went solo, and how going viral with ""Haters Anthem"" motivated the quartet (including sister Momo) to set their sights on even bigger accomplishments.

Along the way, there are plenty of surprises: meeting Oprah and Jon Batiste while busking, stories about 2000s-era Motor City, and more.

videos.title: The Womack Sisters Recall Their Time In Kenya | Questlove Show #shorts
videos.description:
The Questlove Show breaks from its usual one-on-one format to welcome Zeimani, Kucha, and BG—The Womack Sisters. Granddaughters of Sam Cooke and daughters of soul duo Womack & Womack, they released a self-titled album [https://womacksisters.ffm.to/album] on Daptone that’s among Questlove’s favorite records of 2026.

The sisters talk about growing up on tour and living in Ireland, London, Kenya, Thailand, and Paris—including how their father’s intuition helped the family get to safety ahead of the 2004 tsunami. They also discuss years of label rejections and driving for rideshare services while staying true to their sound. Along the way, there are surprises: a photo of Sam Cooke with Questlove’s mother, and Questlove’s story about a Roots show with their uncle, Bobby Womack, that went off the rails.

videos.title: Chuck D | The Questlove Show
videos.description:
In one of the most requested and long-awaited conversations in this show’s history, Chuck D finally joins Questlove in the studio. What unfolds is an intimate conversation about the art, science, and spirit behind Public Enemy—especially during the group’s formative years.

Chuck traces the spark from hearing James Brown's "Blow Your Head" at roller rinks to the Frankenstein tape loops that gave birth to "Public Enemy No. 1," "Rebel Without a Pause," and "Bring the Noise." He recalls writing classic verses on the move, reflects on his early jobs, and breaks down the record-collecting discipline that fueled the Bomb Squad's dense sonic collages.

Along the way, Chuck opens up about aging as an MC, meeting James Brown, and Flavor Flav's evolution. This is Hip-Hop history, music nerdery, and deeply human storytelling from one of Rap's most important and enduring voices.

Chuck D and past QLS guest John Densmore of The Doors have teamed up as do+pe for a new collaborative album, No Country For Old Men [https://bio.to/nocountryforoldmen]. The latest issue of Chuck's Rap Central Station [https://www.silverbackpublishing.rocks/rap-central-station-shop/] publication is available now.

videos.title: Lenny Kaye & Questlove discuss Bob Dylan & More
videos.description:
Before the Ramones and the Sex Pistols, Lenny Kaye was clerking at Village Oldies on Bleecker Street. In 1972, he compiled Nuggets—and its liner notes helped shape the emerging idea of Punk Rock.

Questlove and Lenny nerd out as fellow record obsessives, swapping stories about organizing vinyl, seeing Jimi Hendrix twice, meeting Patti Smith (whom he played bass for ever since), and recording “Piss Factory” in the final 15 minutes of a session at Electric Lady. Lenny also talks about his new solo debut, Goin' Local [https://lennykaye.lnk.to/GoinLocal], out now on Yep Roc. Made for artistic closure, not to chase a trend, the personal, unhurried record came from a simple conviction: “because I’m my favorite artist.” He reflects on creativity, his enduring love of music, and the crates he’s digging through now.

videos.title: John Carpenter's View on Filmmaking After a Long Career In It | The Questlove Show
videos.description:
Questlove sat down with director and composer John Carpenter in Hollywood to discuss Cathedral, a graphic novel [https://stormkingcomics.com/] and Heavy Metal album [https://johncarpentermusic.bandcamp.com/album/cathedral] inspired by a single dream. Carpenter tells how a bongo lesson from his father led to the iconic Halloween theme. He also talks about casting Kurt Russell after their Elvis TV movie, why The Thing was his hardest shoot, and says The Exorcist remains the scariest movie ever made.

Along the way, Carpenter turns the tables and interviews Questlove, sparking a lively debate about The Beatles and whether music has reached “creative diminished returns.” It’s a funny, engaging conversation between two directors who work in different worlds but share a love of making music.

videos.title: Live Performance: Should it Sound Like the Record? | Nat Adderley Jr.
videos.description:
For Nat Adderley Jr., serving as Luther Vandross’ musical director and longtime pianist was one chapter in a remarkable musical life—and a partnership that helped shape the sound of modern R&B. In conversation with Questlove, Nat looks back on making “Never Too Much,” flying in from Houston to play “A House Is Not a Home,” and trying to talk Luther out of recording the Carpenters’ version of “Superstar.” As Vandross is inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, Nat recalls the grandeur of Luther’s stage shows and the loss of drummer Yogi
Horton. He also reflects on how his arrangement of “If This World Were Mine” found new life in Kendrick Lamar’s “Luther.”

The funny, unpredictable conversation also touches on Nat’s new album, Took So Long [https://linktr.ee/natadderleyjr]—his first as a leader and a return to the Jazz roots that run through his family and his work. In a personal full-circle moment, Quest' tells Nat how a
protest song Nat recorded at 15 with his uncle Cannonball Adderley changed his life.

videos.description:
Questlove and JoJo are NOT close friends. They aren’t—or at least, that’s how they approached this conversation: two pals from different genres and generations who have bonded in recent years, sitting down to see what else they might have in common.

For The Questlove Show, the two get into JoJo’s evolution from teen prodigy to Grammy-winning, multi-platinum artist—songwriting camps, vocal discipline, Broadway chops, creative blocks, and what it means to define success on your own terms. JoJo also gets real about periods of feeling low, her family, and why she’s no longer interested in trauma-dumping in the studio—but still wants the music to hit you hard.

And, because this is QLS, we go everywhere: Boston accents, mermaid dreams, theater nerd deep dives, the standards for singing in the age of AI, and the story behind her viral flip of “Marvin’s Room” by Drake.

This is a conversation about craft, resilience, growing up in public, and choosing joy without losing the soul.

Questlove sits down with Soulection [https://www.soulection.com/] founder Joe Kay live backstage at the 2026 Roots Picnic in Philadelphia. videos.title: Eric Benet on QLS
videos.description:
Questlove sits down with R&B icon Eric Benét for a deeply human, wildly musical conversation tracing the singer’s journey from Milwaukee family harmonies to gold plaques and Grammy nominations.

Benét opens up about early sonic imprints like Burt Bacharach, Dionne Warwick, and “Wichita Lineman,” his Alabama and Mobile roots, and how discovering Questlove’s own lineage story reshaped the way he thinks about ancestry, Haiti, and spirituality. The two dig into Prince vs. Michael Jackson, a legendary James Brown clip, and what it really meant to grow up in Milwaukee during the Jeffrey Dahmer years.

Along the way, the longtime friends talk vocal maintenance, the emotional cost of fame, the rise of Neo-Soul, and what Benét would tell his 16-year-old self. videos.title: Barry Manilow on QLS
videos.description:
Barry Manilow pulls up to The Questlove Show for a rare, career-spanning conversation that begins with humble reflections on Williamsburg, Brooklyn, and ends with Hall of Fame accolades, classic jingles, and a recent victory over cancer. Ahmir and Barry trace his path from CBS mailroom kid to music director, arranger, and reluctant frontman who never saw himself as a singer. Manilow breaks down the craft of writing immortal ad hooks, the no-glam reality of the legendary Continental Baths, and why he'll only write songs as a job now. Barry, who released his first album in 15 years, What A Time last month, also opens up about imposter syndrome and working with Bette Midler, Dionne Warwick, and Ron Dante. This episode was taped in April 2026, before the passing of Clive Davis, Barry Manilow's longtime collaborator, who is mentioned throughout the conversation. Manilow is on tour now [https://barrymanilow.com/], performing in arenas across the US and continuing his record-setting Las Vegas residency.

videos.title: Corinne Bailey Rae Live At The Roots Picnic
videos.description:
Questlove catches up with the one and only Corinne Bailey Rae backstage at the 2026 Roots Picnic in Philly for a quick, casual bonus beat episode. Corinne—who guested on Questlove Supreme in 2024 [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rRFJ7_dREyY]—talks about going back to her debut album 20 years later. She explains why she's stretching those songs out on tour so every night goes somewhere new, and how emotional it was to bring Black Rainbows and the story of Harriet Jacobs to the stage. She also walks us through her new children's book, Put Your Records On [https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/710391/put-your-records-on-by-corinne-bailey-rae-illustrated-by-gillian-eilidh-omara/], about a young girl who finds a song for every feeling in an elder's record collection.

Plus she tells us about writing sessions with Amber and Paris of We Are King and the run-up to her first headline show at the Royal Albert Hall on October 26th, so put your records on, y'all, and enjoy.

videos.title: Arthur Baker Pt. 2
videos.description:
We said we’d come back for Part 2—and we did. Arthur Baker, the architect behind “Planet Rock,” “Confusion,” and so much of the ’80s dance-floor sound, returns to The Questlove Show to finish what we started nearly a year ago.

Arthur takes us from carrying crates of vinyl onto airplanes to the Synclavier sessions for Hall & Oates’ Big Bam Boom, the clubs and DJs who shaped his sound, and the Brooklyn studio sessions that led to what he jokingly calls “New Arthur” records with New Order.

He also opens up about Streetwise Records, the making of Beat Street, the story behind “Sun City” and Artists United Against Apartheid, his connections to Miles Davis, Diana Ross, and Little Steven, and why he wrote his memoir, Looking For The Perfect Beat
[https://www.barnesandnoble.com/w/looking-for-the-perfect-beat-arthur-baker/1146640607?ean=9780571387427], for his daughter.

Arthur Baker is back.

videos.title: Wallo267 Breaks Down What Oz & Other Media Get Wrong About Prison | Questlove Show
videos.description:
“If you had to describe prison, how would you describe it?” Wallo’s answer: “The most peaceful place on earth.”

Wallo267 spent 25 years in prison. He tells Questlove why the prison Hollywood portrays is nothing like the one he knew. In his cell, he became fascinated by TV commercials, which led him to study advertising agencies and legendary adman George Lois. Anthony Bourdain became his “travel agent” to a world he couldn’t yet visit.
Wallo recalls a cell block where Frankie Beverly & Maze played from one cell and Tupac from the next—and where respect mattered because “the consequences of disrespect is at its highest level on this earth.” He pushes back on portrayals like Oz, describing the libraries, chess players, jazz musicians, and gardeners he encountered inside. He also makes the case that, after God, marketing is the most powerful force on the planet.

“I was in Yale, not jail. I was in Princeton, not prison. I was in Penn State, not the state pen.”

In this two-part conversation, Wallo267, author of Yes to You, No to Them [https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GT87GY64?tag=usalinktagdefault-20&th=1&psc=1&geniuslink=true], proudly reflects on the joys of life outside prison after nearly a decade—and challenges misconceptions about what happens behind its walls.

videos.title: Arthur Baker tells Questlove the full story behind "Sun City" | Questlove Show
videos.description:
Arthur Baker tells Questlove the full story behind "Sun City," the 1985 anti-apartheid anthem. It began with a conversation with Cyndi Lauper and a song Little Steven Van Zandt had already written. Will Downing was the first voice on it after Steven, and the guest wish list was drawn up on placemats at the Sunrise Diner. It grew into a lineup of Run-DMC, Melle Mel, Kurtis Blow, Bobby Womack, George Clinton, Joey Ramone, Peter Gabriel, Bonnie Raitt, Pete Townshend, Ringo Starr, Gil Scott-Heron and so many more. 

As Arthur recalls, then Miles Davis buzzed Arthur's intercom unannounced and came up with the song's most famous spoken line, and Herbie Hancock, Tony Williams and Ron Carter later played under his solo. This clip also reveals who turned "Sun City" down, its heady music video, and so much more.

Baker's memoir, Looking for the Perfect Beat [https://www.barnesandnoble.com/w/looking-for-the-perfect-beat-arthur-baker/1146640607?ean=9780571387427], is out now.

videos.title: 1000 Voice-notes | Tame Impala on The Questlove Show
videos.description:
Questlove sits down with Tame Impala’s Kevin Parker, the multi-instrumentalist from Perth—one of the most isolated cities on Earth—who spent years letting the world believe his one-man project was a band.

videos.title: E-40 on His Verbal Paintbrush
videos.description:
A real tycoon is in the building. Questlove sits down with Vallejo’s own E-40, the Yay Area legend who was selling records out of his trunk back when getting a major-label deal felt impossible. He built his own label, financed his projects independently, and gave Hip-Hop an entire dictionary of slang and similes. Now, with Turning My Money Over—a historic 40-song quadruple album—Earl Stevens isn’t slowing down.

E-40 talks about growing up on Magazine Street in Vallejo’s Hillside neighborhood, the New York and Bay Area rappers who shaped his voice, and the year at Grambling State that taught him how to make it on his own. He explains how The Click navigated distribution through consignment sheets, mom-and-pop stores, and even rim shops—and how VHS duplication helped change the game for independent artists. 40 Water recalls his dealings with Tupac, advocates for members of the Hieroglyphics crew, and shares how being doubted by a room full of DJs decades ago only pushed him to go harder.

videos.title: The chaos of running your own record label | Arthur Baker on The Questlove Show
videos.description:
We said we’d come back for Part 2—and we did. Arthur Baker, the architect behind “Planet Rock,” “Confusion,” and so much of the ’80s dance-floor sound, returns to The Questlove Show to finish what we started nearly a year ago.

Arthur takes us from carrying crates of vinyl onto airplanes to the Synclavier sessions for Hall & Oates’ Big Bam Boom, the clubs and DJs who shaped his sound, and the Brooklyn studio sessions that led to what he jokingly calls “New Arthur” records with New Order.

He also opens up about Streetwise Records, the making of Beat Street, the story behind “Sun City” and Artists United Against Apartheid, his connections to Miles Davis, Diana Ross, and Little Steven, and why he wrote his memoir, Looking For The Perfect Beat
[https://www.barnesandnoble.com/w/looking-for-the-perfect-beat-arthur-baker/1146640607?ean=9780571387427], for his daughter.

Arthur Baker is back.

videos.title: Wallo267 & Questlove: How Tiny Decisions Reshape Lives
videos.description:
Wallo267 visited The Questlove Show to discuss his latest book, Yes To You, No To Them [https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GT87GY64?tag=usalinktagdefault-20&th=1&psc=1&geniuslink=true]. Instead, he ended up disrupting Ahmir’s day—in the best possible way—with an experiential pep talk that captures why so many people need this book.

The acclaimed Million Dollaz Worth of Game co-host, motivator, and music lover looks back on his journey—one that began just across town from Questlove’s—and how misinformation led him into life-changing circumstances. The two men compare notes on life and discuss how, after a quarter century behind bars, Wallo has spent the past decade embracing freedom to the fullest while cultivating possibility and hard-earned wisdom.

Along the way, Wallo explains his profound appreciation for Anthony Bourdain, challenges Hollywood’s misconceptions about prison, and much more. The result is a vulnerable and deeply powerful episode of QLS—and only the first half of their full conversation.

videos.title: Eric Benét on The Questlove Show | Questlove Show
videos.description:
Questlove sits down with R&B icon Eric Benét for a deeply human, wildly musical conversation tracing the singer’s journey from Milwaukee family harmonies to gold plaques and Grammy nominations.

Benét opens up about early sonic imprints like Burt Bacharach, Dionne Warwick, and “Wichita Lineman,” his Alabama and Mobile roots, and how discovering Questlove’s own lineage story reshaped the way he thinks about ancestry, Haiti, and spirituality. videos.title: JoJo on The Questlove Show
videos.description:
Questlove and JoJo are NOT close friends. They aren’t—or at least, that’s how they approached this conversation: two pals from different genres and generations who have bonded in recent years, sitting down to see what else they might have in common.

For The Questlove Show, the two get into JoJo’s evolution from teen prodigy to Grammy-winning, multi-platinum artist—songwriting camps, vocal discipline, Broadway chops, creative blocks, and what it means to define success on your own terms. This is a conversation about craft, resilience, growing up in public, and choosing joy without losing the soul.

videos.title: Barry Manilow on Clive Davis, Creative Control & Reimagining “Mandy” in One Take | Questlove Show
videos.description:
Recorded just weeks before Clive Davis's passing, Barry Manilow
reflects on negotiating with the legendary executive and one of their
most beloved collaborations. Manilow breaks down the story behind
“Mandy,” which began as a Rock song he didn’t think suited him. After
spending an afternoon changing chords, reworking the title, and
reshaping the song, he uncovered the hidden love ballad that would
become a career-defining hit. The revisions marked a key chapter in
one of the longest-running creative relationships in music—one that
continued decades later, with Davis contributing to Manilow’s latest
album, What A Time.

videos.title: Eric Benet on the first wave of Neo Soul | Questlove Show #shorts
videos.description:
Questlove sits down with R&B icon Eric Benét for a deeply human, wildly musical conversation tracing the singer’s journey from Milwaukee family harmonies to gold plaques and Grammy nominations.

Benét opens up about early sonic imprints like Burt Bacharach, Dionne Warwick, and “Wichita Lineman,” his Alabama and Mobile roots, and how discovering Questlove’s own lineage story reshaped the way he thinks about ancestry, Haiti, and spirituality. The two dig into Prince vs. Michael Jackson, a legendary James Brown clip, and what it really meant to grow up in Milwaukee during the Jeffrey Dahmer years.

Benét breaks down his path from band life to major labels, the making and shelving of Better and Better, how David Foster and Dean Parks helped shape Hurricane, and why songs like “Spend My Life With You” and “Sometimes I Cry” never get old on stage. Along the way, the longtime friends talk vocal maintenance, the emotional cost of fame, the rise of Neo-Soul, and what Benét would tell his 16-year-old self. videos.title: Captain Beefheart Made Kurt Loder Move Differently | Questlove Show #shorts
videos.description:
Legendary music journalist and MTV News icon Kurt Loder [https://x.com/kurt_loder] joins Questlove in the studio for a deep dive into the evolution of rock criticism, music journalism, and pop culture. Loder traces his journey from his early days covering Janis Joplin and Captain Beefheart to his era-defining work at Rolling Stone and MTV News, sharing firsthand memories of punk at CBGB, Prince, and the rise of Hip-Hop into the mainstream.

Kurt opens up about writing Rolling Stone's first major Rap review, chronicling Tina Turner's life and remarkable comeback in book form, and navigating the ethics, responsibility, and influence of the critic's pen. Questlove and Loder also unpack the line between fandom and objectivity, the danger of snap judgments, and how artists like Prince, James Brown, and Joni Mitchell redefined the possibilities of pop music.

This episode is a masterclass in music history, criticism, and culture, told by one of the most trusted voices ever to cover it.

The conversation also explores KEO's ongoing efforts to celebrate the legacy of another fallen friend and cultural innovator whose work helped bridge artistic disciplines and shape the underground Hip-Hop movement.

Infinite respect to KEO.

videos.title: Basquiat, Haring, and Fab 5 Freddy’s Mission To Rewrite Art History | Questlove Show
videos.description:
Hip-hop visionary Fab 5 Freddy joins Questlove for a wide-ranging conversation tracing his journey from Bed-Stuy's Hancock Street to the forefront of music, art, television, and culture. While discussing his memoir, Everybody's Fly [https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/775871/everybodys-fly-by-fab-5-freddy-with-mark-rozzo/], Fab reflects on Brooklyn's mobile disco scene, the origins of sound system culture, graffiti's transformation of subway cars into rolling art galleries, and the experiences that helped shape Hip-Hop's foundation. He also revisits the enduring legacy of Wild Style and Yo! MTV Raps, sharing stories about bringing rap to mainstream television, introducing N.W.A to a national audience, directing a classic Snoop Dogg video, and championing groundbreaking artists as an executive. Along the way, Fab shines a light on the unsung heroes of the graffiti movement, recalls encounters with figures ranging from Malcolm X and Thelonious Monk to Jean-Michel Basquiat and Keith Haring, and discusses how art, music, and advocacy continue to drive cultural change today.

videos.title: Christopher Cross Explains The Powerhouse Writing Origins of Arthur’s Theme  | Questlove Show
videos.description:
Christopher Cross joins Questlove in Hollywood for a deep musician-to-musician conversation about songwriting, studio craftsmanship, and surviving meteoric success. Cross reveals the true origin of Arthur's Theme (Best That You Can Do)and the outlaw mythology behind Ride Like the Wind, while recalling experiences like seeing Jimi Hendrix live, opening for Led Zeppelin, and singing background vocals with Carl Wilson. He breaks down the making of his classic debut album, his obsession with Steely Dan–level precision, and why his later records still matter deeply to him and his core fans. Along the way, Cross shares rare stories about Brian Wilson, Joni Mitchell, Michael McDonald, and Jimmy Page — plus the unforgettable Ginger Baker milk-and-ulcers story. Christopher Cross is currently on tour [https://www.christophercross.com/]

videos.title: Angela Nissel & Questlove Recall the Purchase That Helped Build Okayplayer | Questlove Show
videos.description:
Angela Nissel and Questlove co-founded Okayplayer, the online community that helped redefine how music fans, artists, and creatives connected. In a rabbit-hole chat from The Questlove Show [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0322WeX0B14], the longtime friends look back on the unlikely chain of events that sparked it all: a royalty check, a much-needed wake-up call, and a trip to a big-box electronics store that led to a purchase with far-reaching consequences.

Angela Nissel's newly published memoir, Good Grief, Pass the Bread, Mom Is Dead [https://www.harpercollins.com/products/good-grief-pass-the-bread-mom-is-dead-angela-nissel?variant=43993025413154] is available now.

videos.title: Angela Nissel on Grief, Regret & the Questions We Never Ask | The Questlove Show
videos.description: Author and screenwriter Angela Nissel joins Questlove—her friend of 35 years—to discuss her memoir, Good Grief, Pass the Bread, Mom Is Dead [https://www.harpercollins.com/products/good-grief-pass-the-bread-mom-is-dead-angela-nissel?variant=43993025413154]. Reflecting on her experience as a caregiver, Angela shares what no one told her: to slow down and ask her mother the questions that mattered while there was still time. She opens up about losing her gratitude practice, the matching pajamas she still keeps, the one Luther Vandross song that makes her cry because it was the only time she ever saw her mother break down, and the nursing ID badge that has become a personal shrine. Together, Angela and Ahmir explore memory, grief, and the small objects and moments that continue to connect us to the people we've lost.

videos.title: Thundercat and Doom | Questlove Show #shorts
videos.description:
Thundercat joins Questlove for a wide-ranging, deeply personal conversation that traces his journey from Compton and church gigs to global stages with Flying Lotus, Mac Miller, and beyond. videos.title: Angela Nissel Talks CAPA, Code-Switching & Being a Nerdy Girl in the Hood | Questlove Show
videos.description:
Angela Nissel reflects on reinventing herself as the funny girl in Philadelphia's top public schools and later as a creative writing major at CAPA (the Philadelphia High School for Creative and Performing Arts), where she often felt overshadowed by dancers, actors, and musicians. She and Ahmir discuss code-switching, being a "nerdy girl in the hood," and how years of relentless rewrites in high school quietly prepared her for Hollywood writers' rooms. Along the way, the two compare their very different present-day relationships with Philadelphia's public transit system, SEPTA.

Nissel's memoir, Good Grief, Pass the Bread, Mom Is Dead [https://www.harpercollins.com/products/good-grief-pass-the-bread-mom-is-dead-angela-nissel?variant=43993025413154], is available now.

videos.title: Mickey Guyton on the Questlove Show | Questlove Show #shorts
videos.description:
Black Music Month kicks off in a major way. Mickey Guyton joins Questlove for a deeply personal conversation about carving out space as a Black woman in Country music, from her church roots in Texas to performing on global stages like the Super Bowl and in China. She opens up about her religious upbringing, perfectionism, anxiety, creative burnout, and finding her true audience among marginalized fans who feel seen in her story. Along the way, Mickey and Quest geek out on Brandy, karaoke etiquette, gatekeeping in Country music, and what it really costs to pioneer a lane that didn't exist before.

videos.title: Fab 5 Freddy on Artists Giving Each Other Work | Questlove Show #shorts
videos.description:
Hip-hop visionary Fab 5 Freddy joins Questlove for a wide-ranging conversation tracing his journey from Bed-Stuy's Hancock Street to the forefront of music, art, television, and culture. While discussing his memoir, Everybody's Fly [https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/775871/everybodys-fly-by-fab-5-freddy-with-mark-rozzo/], Fab reflects on Brooklyn's mobile disco scene, the origins of sound system culture, graffiti's transformation of subway cars into rolling art galleries, and the experiences that helped shape Hip-Hop's foundation. He also revisits the enduring legacy of Wild Style and Yo! MTV Raps, sharing stories about bringing rap to mainstream television, introducing N.W.A to a national audience, directing a classic Snoop Dogg video, and championing groundbreaking artists as an executive. Along the way, Fab shines a light on the unsung heroes of the graffiti movement, recalls encounters with figures ranging from Malcolm X and Thelonious Monk to Jean-Michel Basquiat and Keith Haring, and discusses how art, music, and advocacy continue to drive cultural change today.

videos.description:
Black Music Month kicks off in a major way. Mickey Guyton joins Questlove for a deeply personal conversation about carving out space as a Black woman in Country music, from her church roots in Texas to performing on global stages like the Super Bowl and in China. videos.title: James Alexander on Otis Redding | Questlove Show #shorts
videos.description:
James Alexander on Soundcheck and Monitors | Questlove Show #shorts 

James Alexander joins The Questlove Show for a deeply personal conversation tracing his journey from a teenage musician playing segregated clubs in Memphis to becoming a cornerstone of Stax Records and a protégé of Otis Redding. He reflects on the spontaneous creation and lasting impact of “Soul Finger,” the hard realities of 1960s touring, and the business lessons Redding shared about publishing and ownership, before speaking candidly about the 1967 plane crash that claimed Redding and most of The Bar-Kays, a tragedy he narrowly escaped. Alexander recounts the long process of grief and resilience that followed and how he rebuilt the Bar-Kays with vocalist Larry Dodson, shaping a louder, more aggressive funk-rock sound that powered their next chapter. He also reflects on becoming a go-to rhythm section for Stax and beyond, playing on classics for Rufus Thomas, The Staple Singers, and others, the afterlife of “Holy Ghost” and their showstopping set at Wattstax, the realities of 1970s stagecraft, and the band’s constant reinvention and perseverance that keeps The Bar-Kays active and vital to this day.

Check out the Full Episode: https://youtu.be/xb5zvEcobe0

videos.description:
How MonoNeon Turns Clips Into Comedic Funk | Questlove Show

Questlove digs into MonoNeon’s viral videos where he harmonizes and grooves to everyday speech from people like Cardi B and Tiffany Haddish. Mono explains that talking contains real notes and melodic contours, which he discovers by looping the audio and listening for pitch and rhythm. He describes how the early Cardi B clips were the hardest, because they marked the transition from simply mimicking speech melodies to building full-blown songs and danceable grooves around them. Mono also notes that while some subjects have reposted or reacted, he mainly does these pieces for himself as an exercise in creativity and fun.

Colin Kaepernick's Secret Talent | Questlove Show #shorts

On this episode of The Questlove Show, Questlove sits down with Colin Kaepernick live on stage at Web Summit in Qatar for a focused (but abbreviated) conversation about discipline, courage, and purpose. Kaepernick walks through his morning training routine, reflects on his childhood and early athletic ambitions, and examines the influences that shaped his evolution into activism. He speaks about the ongoing work of Know Your Rights Camp, including its response to recent events, and shares how his Lumi platform is designed to expand student engagement, literacy, and AI fluency. The conversation captures where his journey stands a decade after he stepped fully into public activism.

videos.title: Jamie Lee Curtis | Questlove Show
videos.description:
Jamie Lee Curtis sits down with Questlove for an intimate, funny, and deeply motivating conversation about unlocking your greatness. With her signature candor, Jamie reflects on learning to stop shrinking herself and fully embrace her power—and how a recent connection with Quest helped her see that vision more clearly.

In this wide-ranging chat, Jamie shares how she likes to be coached, the surprising lessons she’s learned from her dog, and why she refuses to dwell on the comments. As she prepares for her latest endeavor, Scarpetta, Jamie also opens up about the creative freedom behind projects like Everything Everywhere All at Once, True Lies, A Fish Called Wanda, and The Bear—and what those experiences taught her about trusting the process and owning your voice.

videos.title: Motown vs Memphis Sound | Questlove Show #shorts
videos.description:
Motown vs Memphis Sound | Questlove Show #shorts 

James Alexander joins The Questlove Show for a deeply personal conversation tracing his journey from a teenage musician playing segregated clubs in Memphis to becoming a cornerstone of Stax Records and a protégé of Otis Redding. He reflects on the spontaneous creation and lasting impact of “Soul Finger,” the hard realities of 1960s touring, and the business lessons Redding shared about publishing and ownership, before speaking candidly about the 1967 plane crash that claimed Redding and most of The Bar-Kays, a tragedy he narrowly escaped. Alexander recounts the long process of grief and resilience that followed and how he rebuilt the Bar-Kays with vocalist Larry Dodson, shaping a louder, more aggressive funk-rock sound that powered their next chapter. He also reflects on becoming a go-to rhythm section for Stax and beyond, playing on classics for Rufus Thomas, The Staple Singers, and others, the afterlife of “Holy Ghost” and their showstopping set at Wattstax, the realities of 1970s stagecraft, and the band’s constant reinvention and perseverance that keeps The Bar-Kays active and vital to this day.

Check out the Full Episode: https://youtu.be/xb5zvEcobe0

Mannie Fresh on His Father's DJ Career | Questlove Show #shorts 

Mannie Fresh joins Questlove to trace his journey from a DJ’s son in New Orleans to one of Hip-Hop’s most influential producers. He reflects on the birth of Bounce music, the creation of Cash Money classics like “Ha,” “Back That Azz Up,” “Bling Bling,” and “Still Fly,” working with Teena Marie, and his hopes for a unified Cash Money and No Limit moment. videos.title: The Birth of Bounce: Mannie Fresh Explains How Obscure Songs Became New Orleans Classics
videos.description:
Mannie Fresh gives a masterclass on the creation of New Orleans Bounce music, explaining how an out of town 12" single Showboys’ “Drag Rap” became known as “Trigger Man,” why the 808 section made crowds lose their minds, and how DJs began looping that break to spark call and response chants in the projects. He also breaks down how Derek B’s “Rock the Beat” became another imported record that may have been deemed a commercial failure yet found an everlasting second life in New Orleans.

Selling CDs to Survive | Questlove Show #shorts 

Questlove sits down with Sonic Youth co-founder and avant-garde icon Kim Gordon for a candid, funny, and surprisingly vulnerable conversation about imposter syndrome, the Downtown/No Wave era, and how a visual artist became a profoundly influential bassist, singer, and producer. Kim talks about embracing spontaneity in the studio, discovering dissonance alongside Public Enemy at Greene Street Studios, accidentally launching her solo career [https://kimgordon.lnk.to/playme] with producer Justin Raisen, and navigating motherhood. She also reflects on recently updating her memoir [ https://www.harpercollins.com/products/girl-in-a-band-10th-anniversary-edition-kim-gordon?variant=43707240906786] and her role in the film Chronology of Water. One of music’s enduring arbiters of cool joins The Questlove Show—take heed.

videos.title: James Alexander of The Bar-Kays | Questlove Show
videos.description:
James Alexander joins The Questlove Show for a deeply personal conversation tracing his journey from a teenage musician playing segregated clubs in Memphis to becoming a cornerstone of Stax Records and a protégé of Otis Redding. He reflects on the spontaneous creation and lasting impact of “Soul Finger,” the hard realities of 1960s touring, and the business lessons Redding shared about publishing and ownership, before speaking candidly about the 1967 plane crash that claimed Redding and most of The Bar-Kays, a tragedy he narrowly escaped. Alexander recounts the long process of grief and resilience that followed and how he rebuilt the Bar-Kays with vocalist Larry Dodson, shaping a louder, more aggressive funk-rock sound that powered their next chapter. He also reflects on becoming a go-to rhythm section for Stax and beyond, playing on classics for Rufus Thomas, The Staple Singers, and others, the afterlife of “Holy Ghost” and their showstopping set at Wattstax, the realities of 1970s stagecraft, and the band’s constant reinvention and perseverance that keeps The Bar-Kays active and vital to this day.

videos.description:
Questlove sits down with Sonic Youth co-founder and avant-garde icon Kim Gordon for a candid, funny, and surprisingly vulnerable conversation about imposter syndrome, the Downtown/No Wave era, and how a visual artist became a profoundly influential bassist, singer, and producer. Kim talks about embracing spontaneity in the studio, discovering dissonance alongside Public Enemy at Greene Street Studios, accidentally launching her solo career [https://kimgordon.lnk.to/playme] with producer Justin Raisen, and navigating motherhood. She also reflects on recently updating her memoir [ https://www.harpercollins.com/products/girl-in-a-band-10th-anniversary-edition-kim-gordon?variant=43707240906786] and her role in the film Chronology of Water. One of music’s enduring arbiters of cool joins The Questlove Show—take heed.

Immigrants is just the latest trick

videos.title: Vince Staple’s *BRILLIANT* Kobe Bryant Scheme Breakdown
The Most GENIUS Number Bars in Rap History
videos.description:
From Rakim to Kendrick Lamar, this is the story of hip-hop’s obsession with numbers.

In this episode of Dissect, host Cole Cuchna breaks down the evolution of “number bars” - a lyrical tradition where rappers use math, numeric sequences, and wordplay to showcase technical skill and encode hidden meaning.

Beginning with Rakim’s groundbreaking verse on “My Melody” (1986) - a quatrain built around groups of seven that secretly mirrors his own 21-letter name - we trace how MCs have used numbers as both a mathematical signature and a symbolic device for decades. From Melle Mel’s divine 7-count in “Superrappin” to Jay-Z’s “22 Twos”, Biggie’s “Ten Crack Commandments,” and Mos Def’s “Mathematics,” numbers became an essential part of hip hop tradition and lyricism.

By the 2000s, artists like Lupe Fiasco, J. Cole, JID, Vince Staples, and Kendrick Lamar transformed number schemes into complex storytelling tools. We unpack everything from Lupe’s hidden 3–2–1 countdown on Kanye West’s “Touch the Sky” to Kendrick’s quantum-level equations on “Nosetalgia.”

videos.title: Kendrick Looks in the Mirror and Sees YOU | "Mirror" Breakdown
videos.description:
A dive deep into "Mirror" from Kendrick Lamar's Mr. Morale & the Big Steppers. Serving as a lyrical epilogue to the album’s emotional climax, “Mirror” delivers Kendrick Lamar’s final moral lesson: “I choose me.” With this mantra, Kendrick brings his morality play to a close, rejecting the performance of salvation in favor of spiritual freedom, radical acceptance, and personal peace.

Returning to the character of oklama — “my people” — Kendrick offers listeners the same mirror he used to confront ego, trauma, and public expectation. The result is a parting reflection on self-love, unconditional compassion, and the divine power of choosing yourself.

You'll Learn:

How Kendrick uses the refrain “I choose me” to subvert the savior complex and center inner transformation.

Why “Mirror” functions as a formal epilogue in a morality play structure, and how every character arc is resolved with intention.

What biblical symbolism lies in Kendrick’s repetition of “I choose me,” and how numbers like 6, 7, and 10 frame his spiritual journey.

How Kendrick reframes his “breakup” with culture, fame, and online morality in favor of healing, family, and authenticity.

Why this track represents Kendrick’s most fully realized vision of unconditional love — and the completion of his transformation into Mr. Morale.

Dissect is part of The Ringer podcast network.

Building on the moral ambiguity and backlash explored in “Auntie Diaries,” “Mr. Morale” thrusts Kendrick into the spotlight of introspection. videos.title: Dissecting Kendrick Lamar’s “family ties” Verse
videos.description:
Why Kendrick's line "I am legacy, I come from the 70" is way deeper than it seems.

On the surface, Kendrick is claiming to be influenced by 1970s soul, as he name checks Al Green in the next line, the 70s singer Kendrick’s parents played a lot when he was a kid.

But just BEFORE this line, Kendrick had been on a string of spiritual references - calling himself a prophet and name checking Metatron and Gabriel, two extra biblical archangels.

And the number 70 is also a very significant and recurring biblical number. 70 first appears in the book of Genesis, where there are 70 nations that originally descended from Noah, so 70 is really a number that represents all people in the world, hence Kendrick’s line “I am a legacy, I come from the 70.”

In this one seemingly simple line, Kendrick packages God, the entire human race, his direct family, and the lineage of Black music, all the things that made him who he is.

From Baby Keem and Kendrick Lamar's song "Family Ties."

videos.title: Childish Gambino’s 3005 Video FINALLY Explained
videos.description:
Dissect unpacks the meaning behind Childish Gambino's 3005 music video. Far from a simple love song, 3005 expresses Gambino's existential loneliness on display throughout the world of Because The Internet. Through the video's use of a few key symbols (a decaying teddy bear, ferris wheel) and a unique looping structure, Donald Glover questions our so-called solutions to the existential threats of the world. Finally, we compare 3005 and This Is America, and how Glover uses the same visual technique to convey a similar overall message.

videos.description:

Three of the Bhavishyavani Future Soundz founders – Ashim Ahluwalia, Mukul Deora and Tejas Mangeshkar – share stories of how they mixed foreign and local inspirations together, and the uphill battles of trying to establish a new culture of nightlife in a country undergoing its own cultural and demographic explosion. 

You can read more about Bhavishyavani Future Soundz here...
► https://www.redbullmusicacademy.com/lectures/bhavishyavani-future-soundz

#BhavishyavaniFutureSoundz #DanceGrooves #RedBullMusicAcademy
__________________________

As electronic dance music and rave culture washed over America and England in the ’90s, India still moved to a more traditional nightlife beat that included Goa trance and chart-approved hits. Indian nightlife began to change at the turn of the century when small groups of artists and creatives across the country found ways to showcase the music and aesthetics they’d witnessed abroad. In Mumbai, it was the Bhavishyavani Future Soundz collective who helped kickstart the evolution of the city’s club culture. 

A multimedia collective composed of amateur DJs, film and design professionals, Bhavishyavani Future Soundz threw their first party on May 13, 1999. Over the years visual themes like traditional Indian weddings or politics would mix with sets of jungle, dub techno and live performances by then-upcoming Indian electronic acts such as MIDIval Punditz. Singer and multimedia artist Lina Pereira found a vessel for expression via the alias of Linn Da Quebrada. Emerging from the favelas of São Paulo in 2015, Pereira took inspiration from her friend Lineker, who fronts the soul band Liniker E Os Caramelows, and merged early experience in theater with baile funk. The result has been a blistering sound and presence that aims to confront established notions of race, gender and sexuality by speaking directly to the political embedded in everyday life and actions. In 2018, Linn Da Quebrada released her debut album _Pajubá_ and starred in the documentary _Bixa Travesty_, both of which explore her background, the search for love and the desire to kill the man inside of her in order to be free.

videos.title: DJ Vibe on Lisbon's Early Club Culture and Tribal House | Red Bull Music Academy
videos.description:
► Subscribe to Red Bull Music Academy: https://win.gs/SubscribeRBMA
The DJ behind Portugal's tribal house scene shares stories of Lisbon’s early club culture, how DJs and venues had to operate within existing cultural constrictions and just how Lisbon’s tribal sound made the jump over the Atlantic. 

You can read more on DJ Vibe here...
► https://www.redbullmusicacademy.com/lectures/dj-vibe

#DJVibe #Housemusic #RedBullMusicAcademy
__________________________

In 1980s Lisbon the resident DJ wasn’t simply housewarming for the main act – they were the only act. For António Pereira, AKA DJ Vibe, that meant the ability to stretch selections across genres and styles, entertaining crowds with everything from new wave, disco and slow jams to the new sounds of acid house and rave. The son of a record store owner, Pereira got his break in the city’s burgeoning nightclub scene while still a teenager, eventually becoming the resident at institutions such as Plateau and Kremlin. 

In 1993, after close to a decade behind the decks, Pereira teamed up with Rui Da Silva as the Underground Sound of Lisbon, releasing a string of singles on local label Kaos Records. Inspired by the harder and deeper end of house music, the duo’s “So Get Up” would eventually make its way to New York City and into the hands of Junior Vasquez at the Sound Factory. videos.description:
CLICK CC FOR ENGLISH SUBS.

Techno producer Peder Mannerfelt retraces his steps from teenage bedrooms to Berghain, touching on influences, production and performance approaches and the politics of club culture.

TOPICS:
2:00 - Embracing electronic music and DJ culture 
10:22 - Philosophy of production 
20:30 - Finding excitement and inspiration in live performance

Swedish producer Peder Mannerfelt embraces the versatility of modern production and electronic music through both his collaborations and solo work. Beginning with bad approximations of funk and dreams of drum & bass during high school, Mannerfelt soon realized that the personal computer held more promise than a guitar. Beginning in 2009, he has applied this interest to the more experimental and abstract side of electronic music via Roll The Dice, his duo with Malcolm Pardon, and his own techno-minded alias the Subliminal Kid, as well as contributing production to Fever Ray’s debut album and 2017’s Plunge. Today Mannerfelt runs his own label, exploring contemporary techno, and regularly DJs and performs live.

videos.title: Yury Chernavsky on Becoming Russia’s First Producer | Red Bull Music Academy
videos.description:
Click CC for English subtitles. 

Famed Russian composer and producer Yury Chernavsky discusses his early years on the Russian jazz circuit, discovering production and electronics and creating new music behind the Iron Curtain. #RBMA 

TOPICS: 
4:14 - Early years as a jazz musician and orchestra member 
10:28 - Muslim Magomayev and experimentation in the Russian jazz world
25:53 - The end of the jazz era and moving into production 
39:28 - Electronic experimentation and Banana Islands 

When Yury Chernavsky began work as a music producer in late ’70s USSR, there was little around him to draw inspiration from and so he looked to the advances and innovations happening in the West. His career began in the late ’60s as a jazz musician, playing the violin and saxophone as a member of various orchestras, including ensembles led by Russian jazz stars Oleg Lundstrem and Leonid Utyosov as well as Muslim Magomayev’s State Jazz Orchestra of Azerbaijan. Inspired by Coltrane, Count Basie and Quincy Jones, Chernavsky worked the concert circuit for over a decade before moving into musical direction, composition and production. In the ’80s he emerged as one of Russia’s first modern-day music producers, working with rock and pop groups as well as experimenting with early synthesizer and studio technologies. As one of the founding members of the legendary Detroit techno crew Underground Resistance – alongside Mad Mike Banks and Jeff Mills – Robert Hood’s legacy in the electronic music world is almost peerless. As well as pioneering the minimal techno sound with his 1994 LP Minimal Nation, he’s released on techno mainstays such as Metroplex and Jeff Mills’ Axis label, set up the Hardwax label and operates seminal techno label M-Plant – through which he’s released dozens of his own records, under his own name and as Floorplan. 2013’s Paradise LP as Floorplan was a volt-face in Hood’s musical story; the soulfulness of his minimal sound given new, hot-blooded life. It's this new life that keeps him a key figure in techno today.

Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis are one of the greatest songwriting and producing duo in music history. Meeting on the same ’70s Minneapolis music scene that produced Prince, the pair formed the band Flyte Time, an outfit that would morph into the original line up of one of the most storied funk groups of the era, the Time. By 1983 the duo had begun more actively pursuing songwriting and producing, commencing a series of essential R&B singles for the likes of the S.O.S Band, Cherrelle, Cheryl Lynn, Alexander O’Neal and others. In 1986 they began their now-legendary association with Janet Jackson, producing the Grammy Award-winning LP _Control_, the first of many career-defining efforts over the next three decades. In addition, they have crafted classics for the likes of Force M.D.’s, Sounds of Blackness, New Edition, Human League, George Michael, Usher, and Mary J. Blige.

Drummer, vocalist and serial collaborator Yoshimi Yokata AKA YoshimiO has been an inescapable presence in the Japanese and international experimental rock and avant-garde scene for over 30 years. Hailing from Okayama, YoshimiO began her career in 1986 with the band U.F.O or Die, a side project of experimental vocalist Yamatsuka Eye, before joining Eye’s Boredoms a year later and eventually becoming one of its longest serving members. 

She began releasing music under the name Yoshimi P-We (now YoshimiO) in 1993, all the while collaborating across various projects – the experimental ensemble OOIOO, the Saicobab quartet, which fuses Indian raga traditions with punk and electronic music – and with international musicians including Kim Gordon, Mats Gustafsson, Susie Ibarra and Robert Lowe. While best known as a drummer and vocalist, Yokata also plays the trumpet and keyboard and often works in improvisational contexts.

Over the last 20 years, projects such as GOD, Techno Animal and Ice (all with Godflesh’s Justin Broadrick), King Midas Sound (alongside Roger Robinson and Kiki Hitomi) and some of his latest work with Miss Red and Dylan Carlson of Earth have seen Martin assimilate myriad musical styles – dub, reggae, punk, jazz, hip-hop, dancehall and dubstep, to name a few – and transform them into something truly unique. The one constant across his expansive output is weight: a weight of volume, of bass, of emotion. It's an approach and a philosophy that’s informed just as much by punk as it is by the legendary London soundsystems of Jah Shaka and Aba Shanti-I.

From creating drones in Ableton to using a metal spring as a bass and a metal sheet as percussion, FM Einheit shows how to tap into the freedom of music as a language. 

Named after the abbreviation for the frequency modulation of shortwave radios he used when he first began making music, Einheit immersed himself in the post-punk world of late ’70s Germany before joining Einstürzende Neubauten in the early ’80s as a percussionist. During his time with the influential West Berlin band, Einheit built custom-made instruments, often using metal, and used hammer drills to create new sounds. Live performances would in turn feature dramatic use of the instruments with banging and destruction, which cemented the band’s uncompromising image and set Einheit on his own unique creative path, writing and performing music with unconventional instruments and approaches. It’s hard to overstate the influence of New York City composer Philip Glass. Along with Steve Reich, his minimalist compositions transformed the world of classical music and, eventually, popular music in general. 

Glass’ early epiphanies occurred in Paris during his time in the mid-’60s studying under Nadia Boulanger and in New York when he heard Steve Reich’s “Piano Phase.” These events helped set Glass on a course toward the repetitive, dramatic, and conceptually rigorous style that has become his trademark. 

Throughout the ’70s Glass refined his work, resulting in career-defining compositions like Music In Twelve Parts and Einstein On The Beach. In the process, he became a popular sensation, a serious composer who wasn’t willfully obscure or too difficult to understand. Glass’ stunning soundtrack work for films like The Thin Blue Line and The Hours, and a symphony based on David Bowie’s album Heroes, has only elevated his standing as one of America’s most popular living composers.
